title: Instagram takes on AI copycats as Meta tests Direct, a messaging-only app
excerpt: Instagram adds an ‘original by’ label for copied Reels, as Meta tests Direct, a standalone messaging app, in Türkiye and Thailand.
content_html:
Instagram is giving creators a tool to find and block copies of their Reels. It will also start spotting AI videos that reuse their audio. The tool, announced on Tuesday, was already available on Facebook, TechCrunch reported.

It scans Instagram for unauthorised uses of a creator’s protected videos and sends an alert when it finds a match. The creator can then block the copy on Instagram and Facebook. Or they can add an “original by” label that links back to their video. They can also leave the copy up and track how it performs, or release their claim.

It will also flag AI-generated videos that reuse a creator’s original audio with new visuals. A small group of creators will test that part in the coming weeks. Instagram says it is looking at ways to limit the reach of accounts that keep using AI to repost others’ work.

Eligible creators get a notification in their activity feed. Once they enrol, the tool covers every new video they post, and they can add older ones by hand. They can also add a second profile or a brand to an allow list, so its posts never count as matches.

A day earlier, Meta started testing Direct, a standalone messaging app from Instagram, in Türkiye and Thailand. People can sign up with an email address or phone number, without an Instagram account, Meta said in its announcement.

Instagram users can log in with the same username and password, and their chats sync across both apps. Direct has the same creative tools as Instagram’s inbox, including Draw, Notes, custom Stickers, Voice Effects and chat Themes.

Only a user’s contacts and existing connections can start a chat with them or add them to a group. Users without an Instagram account add contacts by entering an exact username or scanning a QR code in person.

Meta says it will use technology to detect potentially inappropriate interactions with young people. Parents can use its supervision tools to see who their teen messages and set daily time limits. Users must be at least 13. Meta will ask accounts it suspects are younger to verify their age, and delete them if they don’t.

Instagram head Adam Mosseri has often said messaging is the app’s most-used feature, Engadget noted. Meta did not say whether Direct will reach other countries.

Both moves follow Instagram’s launch of Amazon affiliate links in Reels on Monday, and changes to recommendations in India. Meta also widened its AI age checks this month.
